This document provides a detailed mathematical description of the multinomial logit (MNL) model as implemented in `src/mnlogit.cpp`.

## Notation

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $i = 1, \ldots, N$ | Index for individuals (choice situations) |
| $j = 1, \ldots, J_i$ | Index for alternatives available to individual $i$ |
| $C_i$ | Choice set for situation $i$; it contains $M_i=J_i$ inside alternatives and, when requested, the implicit outside alternative 0 |
| $j_i$ | The alternative chosen by individual $i$ |
| $w_i$ | Weight for individual $i$ |
| $X_{ij}$ | Row vector of covariates for individual $i$ and alternative $j$ ($1 \times K$) |
| $\beta$ | Coefficient vector ($K \times 1$) |
| $\delta_j$ | Alternative-specific constant (ASC) for alternative $j$ |
| $V_{ij}$ | Systematic (deterministic) utility |
| $P_{ij}$ | Probability that individual $i$ chooses alternative $j$ |

---

## 1. Model Definition

### 1.1 Utility Specification

The utility that individual $i$ derives from alternative $j$ is:

$$
U_{ij} = V_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$

where the systematic utility is:

$$
V_{ij} = X_{ij}\beta + \delta_j
$$

and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is an i.i.d. Type I Extreme Value (Gumbel) error term with location 0 and scale 1.

### 1.2 Alternative-Specific Constants (ASCs)

The ASC parameters $\delta_j$ capture the average effect of unobserved factors for each alternative. For identification, one ASC must be normalized:

- **Without outside option** (`include_outside_option = FALSE`): The first inside alternative's ASC is fixed to zero ($\delta_1 = 0$). The parameter vector contains $J-1$ free ASC parameters.

- **With outside option** (`include_outside_option = TRUE`): The outside option (alternative 0) has utility $V_{i0} = 0$, serving as the reference. All $J$ inside alternatives have free ASC parameters.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

---

## 2. Log-Likelihood Function

### 2.1 Choice Probability

Under the Type I Extreme Value distribution assumption, the probability that individual $i$ chooses alternative $j$ follows the multinomial logit (softmax) formula:

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(V_{ij})}{\sum_{k=1}^{J_i} \exp(V_{ik})}
$$

If an outside option is included, the denominator includes $\exp(V_{i0}) = \exp(0) = 1$.
The outside option is implicit: it has no row in $X$, no free coefficient, and is
prepended internally to the vector of inside utilities.  Global alternative IDs
(`alt_idx`) need not equal an alternative's local row position in $C_i$; the former map
ASCs across situations, whereas `choice_idx` records the local chosen position (or 0 for
the outside option).

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

### 2.2 Log-Likelihood

The log-likelihood is the weighted sum of the log-probabilities of the observed choices:

$$
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \log P_{ij_i}
$$

where $\theta = (\beta, \delta)$ is the full parameter vector and $j_i$ is the alternative chosen by individual $i$.

Expanding the log-probability:

$$
\log P_{ij_i} = V_{ij_i} - \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^{J_i} \exp(V_{ik})\right)
$$

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

### 2.3 Log-Sum-Exp Trick for Numerical Stability

To prevent numerical overflow when computing the denominator, the implementation subtracts the maximum utility before exponentiation:

$$
\sum_k \exp(V_{ik}) = \exp(V_{\max}) \sum_k \exp(V_{ik} - V_{\max})
$$

where $V_{\max} = \max_k V_{ik}$.

This gives:

$$
\log\left(\sum_k \exp(V_{ik})\right) = V_{\max} + \log\left(\sum_k \exp(V_{ik} - V_{\max})\right)
$$

The log-probability becomes:

$$
\log P_{ij_i} = (V_{ij_i} - V_{\max}) - \log\left(\sum_k \exp(V_{ik} - V_{\max})\right)
$$

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

---

## 3. Gradient Computation

### 3.1 General Formula

The gradient of the log-probability of the chosen alternative with respect to utility is:

$$
\frac{\partial \log P_{ij_i}}{\partial V_{ia}} = \mathbf{1}_{a = j_i} - P_{ia}
$$

where $\mathbf{1}_{a = j_i}$ is the indicator function (1 if $a$ is the chosen alternative, 0 otherwise).

### 3.2 Gradient with Respect to $\beta$

Since $\frac{\partial V_{ij}}{\partial \beta} = X_{ij}^T$, the contribution to the gradient from individual $i$ is:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \beta} = w_i \sum_{j=1}^{J_i} \left(\mathbf{1}_{j = j_i} - P_{ij}\right) X_{ij}^T
$$

This simplifies to:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \beta} = w_i \left( X_{ij_i}^T - \sum_{j=1}^{J_i} P_{ij} X_{ij}^T \right)
$$

The full gradient is:

$$
\nabla_\beta \ell = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \left( X_{ij_i}^T - \sum_{j=1}^{J_i} P_{ij} X_{ij}^T \right)
$$

**Implementation note.** Define the difference vector $d_i \in \mathbb{R}^{J_i}$ with entries $d_{ij} = \mathbf{1}_{j = j_i} - P_{ij}$. Then the sum above is $X_i^T d_i$, a single BLAS matrix-vector product (`X_i.t() * diff_vec`). When an outside option is present, $X_i$ covers only the $M_i$ inside alternatives and $d_i$ is sliced accordingly (`diff_vec.subvec(1, m_i)`).

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

### 3.3 Gradient with Respect to $\delta$

Since $\frac{\partial V_{ij}}{\partial \delta_a} = \mathbf{1}_{j = a}$, the contribution to the gradient from individual $i$ for alternative $a$ is:

$$
\frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \delta_a} = w_i \left(\mathbf{1}_{j_i = a} - P_{ia}\right)
$$

The gradient is computed only for the free ASC parameters:
- Without outside option: $\delta_1 = 0$ (fixed), so we compute for $a = 2, \ldots, J$
- With outside option: we compute for all inside alternatives $a = 1, \ldots, J$

The delta gradient reuses the same difference vector $d_i$ computed for the beta block; its entries are scattered into the appropriate positions of the gradient vector via an irregular index mapping.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

---

## 4. Hessian Computation

### 4.1 Analytical Hessian — Full-Vector Form

The Hessian of the log-likelihood for individual $i$ is:

$$H_i = \frac{\partial^2 \ell_i}{\partial \theta \,\partial \theta'} = -w_i \left[ \sum_{a \in A_i} P_{ia} Z_a Z_a^T - \left(\sum_{a \in A_i} P_{ia} Z_a\right)\left(\sum_{a \in A_i} P_{ia} Z_a\right)^T \right]$$

where $A_i$ is individual $i$'s choice set (including the outside option when present) and $Z_a \in \mathbb{R}^{K + J_\delta}$ is the "score vector" for alternative $a$:

$$Z_a = \begin{pmatrix} x_a \\ e_{d(a)} \end{pmatrix}$$

Here $x_a \in \mathbb{R}^K$ is the covariate vector for alternative $a$, $e_{d(a)}$ is the standard basis vector in $\mathbb{R}^{J_\delta}$ indicating the free ASC position $d(a)$ for alternative $a$, and $J_\delta$ is the number of free ASC parameters ($J-1$ without outside option, $J$ with outside option). For the outside option itself, $Z_0 = 0$ (no covariates, no free ASC).

This can be written compactly as:

$$H_i = -w_i \operatorname{Var}_{P_i}(Z)$$

where the variance is taken under the discrete distribution $P_i = (P_{i0}, P_{i1}, \ldots, P_{iJ_i})$. The full Hessian is $\nabla^2_\theta \ell = \sum_{i=1}^N H_i$ and the function returns $-\nabla^2_\theta \ell$ (Hessian of the negative log-likelihood).

### 4.2 Block Decomposition

The parameter vector is $\theta = (\beta, \delta)$ with $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^K$ (covariate coefficients) and $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^{J_\delta}$ (free ASC parameters). Because $Z_a$ has at most $K+1$ nonzero entries — $K$ in the $\beta$ block and at most one in the $\delta$ block — the dense $n_\mathrm{params} \times n_\mathrm{params}$ outer product $Z_a Z_a^T$ has only three nontrivial submatrices. Summing over alternatives, the individual Hessian decomposes into three blocks:

$$-H_i / w_i = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{BB}_i & \mathbf{BD}_i \\ \mathbf{BD}_i^T & \mathbf{DD}_i \end{pmatrix}$$

**Beta-beta block** ($K \times K$, symmetric):

$$\mathbf{BB}_i = \sum_{a=1}^{m_i} p_{ia} \, x_a x_a^T - \mu_\beta \mu_\beta^T, \qquad \mu_\beta = \sum_{a=1}^{m_i} p_{ia} \, x_a$$

where the sum runs over the $m_i$ inside alternatives only (since $Z_0 = 0$). This is the probability-weighted covariance of the covariates:

$$\mathbf{BB}_i = \mathbb{E}_{P_i}[x x^T] - \mathbb{E}_{P_i}[x]\, \mathbb{E}_{P_i}[x]^T = \operatorname{Cov}_{P_i}(x)$$

**Delta-delta block** ($J_\delta \times J_\delta$, symmetric):

$$\mathbf{DD}_i = \operatorname{diag}(\mu_\delta) - \mu_\delta \mu_\delta^T, \qquad \mu_\delta[r] = \sum_{\{a : d(a)=r\}} p_{ia}$$

When a situation lists an alternative once, $\mu_\delta[r]$ is that alternative's choice probability; rows that repeat an alternative add their probabilities into its one entry. The diagonal of $\mathbf{DD}_i$ is $\mu_\delta \odot (1 - \mu_\delta)$ and the off-diagonal $(r,s)$ entry is $-\mu_\delta[r]\,\mu_\delta[s]$; $\mu_\delta$ is zero off the constants of the alternatives the situation offers.

**Beta-delta block** ($K \times J_\delta$, generally not symmetric):

$$\mathbf{BD}_i[:,r] = \sum_{\{a : d(a)=r\}} p_{ia} \, x_a - \mu_\beta \, \mu_\delta[r]$$

This block measures the probability-weighted covariance between the covariates and the ASC indicators.

**Why the decomposition equals the full-vector form.** Partition $Z_a = (x_a^T, e_{d(a)}^T)^T$. Then:

$$\sum_a p_{ia} Z_a Z_a^T = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_a p_{ia} x_a x_a^T & \sum_a p_{ia} x_a e_{d(a)}^T \\ \sum_a p_{ia} e_{d(a)} x_a^T & \sum_a p_{ia} e_{d(a)} e_{d(a)}^T \end{pmatrix}$$

$$\left(\sum_a p_{ia} Z_a\right)\left(\sum_a p_{ia} Z_a\right)^T = \begin{pmatrix} \mu_\beta \mu_\beta^T & \mu_\beta \mu_\delta^T \\ \mu_\delta \mu_\beta^T & \mu_\delta \mu_\delta^T \end{pmatrix}$$

Subtracting block by block yields exactly $\mathbf{BB}_i$, $\mathbf{BD}_i$, $\mathbf{DD}_i$ above.

### 4.3 Compact Blocks and Accumulation

Because $\mu_\delta$ is zero off the situation's own constants, $\mathbf{BD}_i$ and
$\mathbf{DD}_i$ vanish outside them: situation $i$'s Hessian lives on its *compact block*,
the $K$ coefficients and the $a_i \le m_i$ free constants of the alternatives it offers
(in increasing order). The kernel forms $\mathbf{BB}_i$ (its upper triangle),
$\mathbf{BD}_i$ ($K \times a_i$) and the constants' block ($a_i \times a_i$, from the
vector $\mu_\delta$ as it is added) and adds $w_i$ times them into the upper triangle of
an $n \times n$ accumulator, which is mirrored once after the loop. A situation costs
$O(m_iK^2 + a_iK + a_i^2)$, whatever the number of alternatives $J$; adding its dense
$\mathbf{BD}_i$ and $\mathbf{DD}_i$ cost $O(KJ_\delta + J_\delta^2)$, which dominated with
thousands of constants (281 s for 24,560 situations and 2,611 parameters at one thread,
against 0.13 s for the compact blocks).

Each thread adds into its own packed upper triangle while the threads' triangles fit in a
budget (2 GiB by default; the kernels' internal `acc_bytes`), and above it into the shared
result: the coefficients' rows through small private buffers, the constants' block by
atomic additions. Both are allocated before the parallel loop, and the kernel first
compares an upper estimate of its memory with `options(choicer.max_memory)` or the
machine's physical memory, stopping with an error that names the number of threads that
fits.

**Non-finite values.** The dense form subtracted $\mu\mu^T$ over every parameter, so a
non-finite mean (overflowing utilities, a covariate near the largest double) reached its
row's entries outside the block as $0 \cdot \text{mean}$, NaN; and a non-finite weight
multiplied the zeros outside the block. The compact kernel adds those values where the
dense form did: the spread of a non-finite mean during the loop (once per row and thread
for a NaN mean, which turns the whole row NaN), and the spread of a non-finite weight
after it.

### 4.4 ASC Normalization and Indexing

The free-delta position $d(a)$ for inside alternative $a$ (0-based local index within individual $i$'s choice set, with $a \in \{0,\ldots,m_i-1\}$) is:

$$d(a) = \begin{cases} \text{alt\_idx0\_i}[a] & \text{if } \texttt{include\_outside\_option} = \text{TRUE} \\ \text{alt\_idx0\_i}[a] - 1 & \text{if } \texttt{include\_outside\_option} = \text{FALSE and alt\_idx0\_i}[a] > 0 \\ \text{(skip — no ASC contribution)} & \text{if } \texttt{include\_outside\_option} = \text{FALSE and alt\_idx0\_i}[a] = 0 \end{cases}$$

where `alt_idx0_i[a]` is the 0-based global alternative ID from `alt_idx0`. When there is no outside option, the first inside alternative ($\text{alt\_idx0\_i}[a] = 0$) has its ASC fixed to zero by the identification convention, so it contributes no free ASC entry and is skipped in the BD and DD accumulation.

**Implementation note.** Each term is formed as the dense form formed it — every product
of means rounded before it is subtracted — and added in the same order, so at one thread
the compact Hessian is the dense one bit for bit, except where the dense form's BLAS call
fused a product into the subtraction (in designs with a single coefficient or a single
constant), where the two differ in their last bits.

*Code reference: `src/mnlogit.cpp`, function `mnl_loglik_hessian_parallel`.*

## 5. Elasticity Computation

### 5.1 Elasticity Definitions

The elasticity measures the percentage change in choice probability with respect to a percentage change in an attribute. For attribute $k$ with coefficient $\beta_k$:

**Own-Elasticity** (elasticity of $P_{ij}$ with respect to $x_{ijk}$):

$$
E_{jj}^k = \frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{ijk}} \cdot \frac{x_{ijk}}{P_{ij}} = \beta_k \cdot x_{ijk} \cdot (1 - P_{ij})
$$

**Cross-Elasticity** (elasticity of $P_{ij}$ with respect to $x_{imk}$ where $m \neq j$):

$$
E_{jm}^k = \frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{imk}} \cdot \frac{x_{imk}}{P_{ij}} = -\beta_k \cdot x_{imk} \cdot P_{im}
$$

### 5.2 Derivation

Starting from the choice probability:

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{\exp(V_{ij})}{\sum_k \exp(V_{ik})}
$$

Taking the derivative with respect to $x_{imk}$:

$$
\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{imk}} = P_{ij} \left( \mathbf{1}_{j=m} - P_{im} \right) \beta_k
$$

For own-elasticity ($j = m$):

$$
\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{ijk}} = P_{ij} (1 - P_{ij}) \beta_k
$$

Therefore:

$$
E_{jj}^k = \beta_k \cdot x_{ijk} \cdot (1 - P_{ij})
$$

For cross-elasticity ($j \neq m$):

$$
\frac{\partial P_{ij}}{\partial x_{imk}} = -P_{ij} P_{im} \beta_k
$$

Therefore:

$$
E_{jm}^k = -\beta_k \cdot x_{imk} \cdot P_{im}
$$

### 5.3 Weighted Average of Individual Elasticities

The implementation computes a weighted average of the *individual probability
elasticities*:

$$
\bar{E}_{jm}^k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \cdot E_{ijm}^k}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}
$$

where $E_{ijm}^k$ is the elasticity for individual $i$.

This estimand is not, in general, the elasticity of the aggregate share
$s_j=\sum_iw_iP_{ij}/\sum_iw_i$.  The latter is

$$
\frac{\partial s_j}{\partial x_{m,k}}\frac{x_{m,k}}{s_j},
$$

and requires a definition of the common market-level perturbation $x_{m,k}$ when the
attribute varies over individuals.  `elasticities()` deliberately reports the average
of individual elasticities above; rows index responding alternatives and columns index
perturbed alternatives.  With an outside option, index 0 is included in the returned
matrix; its attribute value is zero, so the outside-option perturbation column is zero.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

## 6. Diversion Ratio Computation

### 6.1 Definition

The diversion ratio from alternative $j$ to alternative $k$ measures the fraction of demand lost by $j$ that is captured by $k$ when $j$ becomes less attractive (e.g., due to a price increase). It is a key metric in antitrust analysis and merger simulation.

$$
DR(j \to k) = -\frac{\partial Q_k / \partial p_j}{\partial Q_j / \partial p_j}
$$

where $Q_j = \sum_i w_i P_{ij}$ is the (weighted) aggregate demand for alternative $j$ and $p_j$ is the price of $j$.

### 6.2 Derivation for MNL

From the MNL choice probability derivatives (Section 5.2), the demand derivatives with respect to price $p_j$ (with coefficient $\beta_p$) are:

$$
\frac{\partial Q_k}{\partial p_j} = -\beta_p \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik} \quad (k \neq j)
$$

$$
\frac{\partial Q_j}{\partial p_j} = \beta_p \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij} \, (1 - P_{ij})
$$

Substituting into the diversion ratio formula:

$$
DR(j \to k) = -\frac{-\beta_p \sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik}}{\beta_p \sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, (1 - P_{ij})} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik}}{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, (1 - P_{ij})}
$$

The price coefficient $\beta_p$ cancels, so the diversion ratio does not depend on which covariate we differentiate with respect to. This is a consequence of the IIA property.

### 6.3 Aggregate Diversion Ratio Matrix

The implementation computes the full $J \times J$ diversion ratio matrix $D$ where:

$$
D_{kj} = DR(j \to k) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \, P_{ij} \, (1 - P_{ij})} \quad (k \neq j)
$$

$$
D_{jj} = 0
$$

### 6.4 Properties

**Column sums equal one.** For a given alternative $j$, the off-diagonal entries in column $j$ sum to 1, meaning all diverted demand is accounted for:

$$
\sum_{k \neq j} DR(j \to k) = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \sum_{k \neq j} P_{ik}}{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} (1 - P_{ij})} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} (1 - P_{ij})}{\sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} (1 - P_{ij})} = 1
$$

where we used $\sum_{k \neq j} P_{ik} = 1 - P_{ij}$.

**IIA proportionality.** When all individuals face the same choice set and the same covariates (so $P_{ij}$ does not vary across $i$), the diversion ratio simplifies to:

$$
DR(j \to k) = \frac{P_j \, P_k}{P_j (1 - P_j)} = \frac{P_k}{1 - P_j} = \frac{s_k}{1 - s_j}
$$

where $s_j$ is the market share of alternative $j$. This means diversion is proportional to the receiving alternative's market share, independent of any characteristics of the losing alternative $j$ other than its own share. This is a well-known limitation of MNL due to IIA.

### 6.5 Implementation

The function accumulates two quantities in parallel across individuals:

1. **Numerator matrix**: $N_{kj} = \sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, P_{ik}$ for each pair $(k, j)$
2. **Denominator vector**: $d_j = \sum_i w_i \, P_{ij} \, (1 - P_{ij})$ for each $j$

The final matrix is computed as $D_{kj} = N_{kj} / d_j$ for $k \neq j$, with $D_{jj} = 0$,
in place in the numerator's $J \times J$ sum (§12.3); a column whose denominator is at most
$10^{-15}$ (an alternative no situation offers, say) is set to zero.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

## 7. BLP Share Inversion

### 7.1 Problem Statement

Given target market shares $S_j$ (with an outside option, $S_0$ too, all of them summing to
one), find the alternative-specific constants $\delta$ at which the model's predicted
shares equal them, with $\beta$ held at its value:

$$
\hat{s}_j(\delta) = \frac{\sum_i w_i P_{ij}(\delta)}{\sum_i w_i} = S_j \quad \forall j
$$

where $\hat{s}_j(\delta)$ is the predicted market share for alternative $j$. With every
alternative available in every choice situation, any interior target is attained by a
unique $\delta$, up to the normalization below (Berry 1994). Where choice sets differ,
attainability restricts the targets (§7.2); a solution, where it exists, is still unique
up to that normalization, the logit's shares being connected substitutes (Berry, Gandhi
and Haile 2013).

### 7.2 Identification and Checks of the Targets

With an outside option, whose utility is normalized to zero, every inside constant is
identified. Without one, the shares depend only on differences of constants among
alternatives that share choice situations, directly or through others: each such group (a
connected component of the graph that links the alternatives through the choice
situations of positive weight) identifies its constants up to a common level, and its
shares add up to the weight of its situations. Each component's reference, its smallest
alternative code, is held at its start, after the start is normalized by subtracting its
first element, so that the first constant is zero.

Targets that no constants attain stop the inversion before any evaluation of the shares,
with an error: an alternative offered in no choice situation of positive weight; targets
that do not sum to one (the outside share included), or, without an outside option, a
component's targets that do not add up to its situations' weight, within a relative
$1.5 \times 10^{-8}$ (within it they are rescaled); targets that leave no share to the
outside option in a component; and a target not strictly below the weight of the choice
situations that offer the alternative, or, without an outside option, not strictly above
the weight of those that offer it alone (an alternative alone in its component is exempt:
its share is its situations' weight). These are necessary conditions: a target that passes
them may still be unattainable, and the iteration then does not converge.

### 7.3 The Iteration

Write $r = \log S - \log \hat{s}(\delta)$ for the log-share residuals and $b$ for the base:
the outside option, or, without one, the reference of $j$'s component. The free constants
solve $\rho_j(\delta) = r_j - r_b = 0$; with an outside option, $r_j - r_0$ is the
outside-share correction of Fukasawa (2024). Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes's (1995)
contraction, `method = "original"`, updates $\delta_j \leftarrow \delta_j + r_j$ (with the
component's reference held, $\delta_j + r_j - r_b$).

The derivative of $\rho$ in the free constants is

$$
-\frac{\partial \rho_j}{\partial \delta_k}
= \frac{1}{\hat{s}_j}\frac{\partial \hat{s}_j}{\partial \delta_k} + \frac{C_{kb}}{\hat{s}_b},
\qquad
A_{jj} = \frac{\partial \hat{s}_j}{\partial \delta_j}
= \frac{\sum_i w_i P_{ij}(1 - P_{ij})}{\sum_i w_i},
\qquad
C_{jb} = -\frac{\partial \hat{s}_b}{\partial \delta_j}
= \frac{\sum_i w_i P_{ij} P_{ib}}{\sum_i w_i}:
$$

a part with a dominant diagonal, $A_{jj}/\hat{s}_j$, plus a term common to every row, the
response of the base's share. The step, `method = "simple"`, treats the two in
turn. A common shift $\tau$ of the component's free constants moves each $\rho_j$ by
$-h_j \tau$ to first order, where $h_j = C_{jb}/\hat{s}_j + \sum_k C_{kb}/\hat{s}_b$
exactly (the share Jacobian is symmetric and its rows sum to zero), and $\tau$ solves
$\sum_j \hat{s}_j (\rho_j - h_j \tau) = 0$, to first order the shift that matches the
base's share. The rest of each residual takes the exact diagonal of the derivative:

$$
\delta_j \leftarrow \delta_j + \tau + \frac{\rho_j - h_j \tau}{D_j},
\qquad
D_j = \frac{A_{jj}}{\hat{s}_j} + \frac{C_{jb}}{\hat{s}_b}.
$$

The diagonal alone misjudges the common shift. Where the base's share is small and each
alternative dominates choice situations of its own, $1 - h_j/D_j$ falls below $-1$ and
that step diverges where Berry's contraction converges: in three choice situations, each
won by one of alternatives 2 to 4 ($x'\beta$ of 3 for the winner, $-3$ for the other two
and 0 for a rarely chosen alternative 1, with constants $(0, 1, 1, 1)$), it is $-1.82$ at
the solution. A choice situation that lists an alternative twice contributes its total
probability. One evaluation of the shares gives $\hat{s}$, $A$ and $C$ together.

Safeguards keep the step from failing where Berry's contraction converges. A step is at
most $\max(|\rho_j|, 5)$ in magnitude: the scaling may lengthen the unscaled step
$\rho_j$ to 5 log units, not beyond (an alternative chosen almost wherever it is offered
has a diagonal near zero). In an iteration where a component's outside share underflows
to zero, the step drops the outside correction and the common shift ($r_j$ over
$A_{jj}/\hat{s}_j$). An evaluation whose shares are not finite halves the step, up to ten
times. An iteration whose best residual has not improved for 30 iterations (a stall)
halves its later steps. If its residual at the stall is more than twice the best, the
steps diverge, and it first returns to its best point, once per best point; otherwise it
goes on from where it is, each such stall doubling the iterations the next one waits for.
Going on matters: far from the solution the common shift can strand constants where their
shares barely respond (alternatives offered with the base only in situations that others
dominate), and the way back can climb for dozens of iterations at a residual above the
best so far, a climb that returning to that best point at every stall would never
complete. And the scaling can amplify a small residual of an alternative that nearly owns
its choice situations, whose diagonal is near zero, into a step that wrecks the shares of
its neighbours there; the two then oscillate, and the residual decays too slowly. Berry's
contraction never amplifies a step, so it races the step once the step stops making
progress: when 100 iterations fail to halve the best residual (or a trial point's shares
stay non-finite after every halving, and the step stops), the contraction starts from the
same start and the two take steps in turn, each with its halvings. The first to reach the
tolerance returns. The contraction stops if 100 of its own evaluations of the shares fail
to halve its best residual while the step's best is lower; the step then has 200
iterations at a time to halve its own best residual, and whenever it fails to, the
contraction goes on from where it stopped: the step can also carry the constants of
alternatives that make up the whole choice set of some choice situations so far down that
the residual barely responds to their common level, and then make no progress at all.
Where the contraction converges in $E$ evaluations, the step converges within $T + 4E$,
and within $T + 2E$ where the contraction halves its best residual within every 100 of
its evaluations, $T$ being the evaluations before the contraction joined; the bound
leaves out the step's halvings after the contraction joined and any 200 iterations in
which the step alone halved its best residual. Berry's contraction itself, as `method =
"original"`, takes only the halving of steps whose shares are not finite.

`method = "anderson"`, the default, accelerates the same step, Anderson acceleration of
type II (Walker and Ni 2011). Write $f(\delta)$ for the step at $\delta$, and $\Delta X$ and $\Delta F$
for the last $m$ differences (`memory`, default 10, cut to the number of free constants)
between successive iterates and between their steps, newest first. Each iteration solves
the least squares
$\min_\gamma \|f - \Delta F \gamma\|_2$, the combination of past changes in the step that
best cancels the current one, and moves to

$$
\delta \leftarrow \delta - \Delta X \gamma + \left(f - \Delta F \gamma\right),
$$

the capped step above while there are no differences. On a linear map, undamped and with
unlimited memory, this is essentially GMRES (Walker and Ni 2011), so it handles the slow
modes of segmented choice sets that the step alone crawls along. The least squares go through a Householder QR of $\Delta F$,
one per iteration, and the oldest differences are dropped while the triangular factor's
condition estimate, $\max_i |R_{ii}| / \min_i |R_{ii}|$, exceeds `max_condition`
(default $10^8$). Its safeguards are on the residual, never on a merit function: when
five iterations bring no residual below 0.9 times the best so far, or the shares at an
extrapolated point are not finite, it clears its differences and takes the plain step
from where it is, halved while its shares are not finite; only where its residual has
grown past twice the best does it go back to its best point, once per best point, since
a path to the solution can climb through larger residuals first (the step's stalls
above). Where a component's outside share underflows it takes the step unextrapolated,
keeping no differences, until the share returns: the step then has another form (no
outside correction, no common shift), and its level drifts by about the same amount at
every iteration, which the least squares would try to cancel instead of follow. It races
the contraction like the step, each of its iterations one evaluation of
the shares besides trial points whose shares are not finite (left out of the bound, as
the step's halvings are), so the bound $T + 4E$ holds for it too.

`method = "squarem"` extrapolates the step by SQUAREM (Varadhan and Roland 2008), PyBLP's
default. With $G(\delta) = \delta + f(\delta)$, each cycle takes $\delta_1 = G(\delta_0)$
and $\delta_2 = G(\delta_1)$, sets $r = \delta_1 - \delta_0$ and
$v = \delta_2 - 2\delta_1 + \delta_0$, and moves to

$$
\delta_0 + 2\alpha r + \alpha^2 v,
\qquad
\alpha = \|r\|_2 / \|v\|_2
$$

(`scheme` 3; scheme 1 takes $-r'v/v'v$, scheme 2 $-r'r/r'v$), bounded to [`step_min`,
`step_max`], 1 and 1 at first; one more step $G$ from that point starts the next cycle.
Each time $\alpha$ reaches `step_max` at a point whose residual is finite, the bound is
multiplied by `step_factor` (4), so the extrapolation lengthens while it succeeds; where
the shares at an extrapolated point are not finite, the cycle takes $\delta_2$ instead,
and a bound $\alpha$ had reached is divided by `step_factor`, not below its start. With
these bounds it never steps shorter than $\delta_2$, so it cannot damp an oscillating step
as Anderson's least squares can. It races the contraction too.

On the 121 simulated designs of choicer's test bed (multinomial, nested and mixed logits;
2 to 5,000 alternatives; full, regional and chained choice sets; far starts), solved to
$10^{-12}$, the step converged on every one; where Berry's contraction converged too (113
designs), the step needed a median 0.36 of its evaluations, and never more than 1.05
times as many; no iteration stalled, and the contraction never joined. On 80 designs
built like the example above, solved to $10^{-10}$, it did not converge within 3,000
evaluations on one, which it was still approaching (it took 9,472, the contraction's
turns included), and Berry's contraction failed on 22; where both converged, the step
needed a median 0.16 of Berry's evaluations. On 999 small designs drawn to be hard (3 to
6 alternatives in 2 to 8 choice situations of random sizes, single-alternative ones
included; covariates and constants integers in $[-10, 10]$ and $[-3, 3]$; half with an
outside option), at tolerance $10^{-8}$ and 1,000 evaluations, the step failed on 103
and Berry's contraction on 592, never where the contraction converged; where both
converged, the step needed a median 0.12 of the contraction's evaluations.

With `method = "anderson"` the same 121 designs converged in medians of 13, 12 and 16.5
evaluations for the multinomial, nested and mixed logits (32, 18.5 and 174 with
`"simple"`), never more than 1.25 times `"simple"`'s, and the 24-alternative market of
four regions from 10 far starts in 27 to 36 evaluations, where `"simple"` needed 3,143
to 3,655. On the 999 small hard designs above and 999 more drawn alike it failed on 61,
29 and 20 at 1,000, 20,000 and 200,000 evaluations, against 210, 80 and 39 for
`"simple"`, and needed a median 0.45 to 0.48 of `"simple"`'s evaluations where both
converged. On simulated claims-, census- and small-scale data (up to $10^7$ rows), at
tolerance $10^{-8}$, it took 0.25 to 1.03 times `"simple"`'s time, which made it the
default.

### 7.4 Stopping Rule and Result

The iteration stops at the first evaluation whose residual is at most `tol` (default
$10^{-12}$), and returns that point. The residual is $\max_j |r_j - r_{b(j)}|$ without an
outside option, $b(j)$ the reference of $j$'s component, and with one $\max_j |r_j|$
together with each component's outside share's $|r_{0c}|$; every share, the outside
option's included, then matches its target to a relative error of about `tol`. The error
in $\delta$
is of order `tol` times the conditioning of the share equations, which choice sets with
few alternatives in common can raise to hundreds or more.

`max_iter` counts evaluations of the shares (default 1,000; 0 returns the normalized start).
When the iteration stops otherwise, at `max_iter` or at shares that are not finite, it
returns the evaluated point of smallest residual and warns with class
`choicer_blp_unconverged`; the condition's `convergence` element holds the status, the
iterations, the evaluations and the residual.

### 7.5 The Layout of `delta`

1. **No outside option.** `delta` has length $J$ (the `blp()` method prepends the
   normalized zero to the fitted length-$(J-1)$ ASC block), and the returned vector's first
   element is zero; it is not the length-$(J-1)$ free-parameter block.
2. **Outside option.** The supplied and returned `delta` have length $J$ and contain the
   inside alternatives only; `target_shares` has $J + 1$ entries, the outside option's
   first.
3. **`blp()`.** The method checks the targets in R first (one share per alternative,
   finite, positive, summing to one), starts from the fitted constants (or `delta_init`),
   and returns the $J \times 1$ matrix with the inside alternatives' labels as row names
   and the attribute `"convergence"`: the record of §7.4 (converged, status, iterations,
   evaluations, residual, `tol` and method), there whether or not the iteration
   converged. The exported functions return the bare matrix.

*Code reference: [src/blp_engine.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/blp_engine.h)
(the components, the checks, the step and the stopping rule),
[src/fixed_point.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/fixed_point.h)
(the iteration), `MnlBlpModel` in
[src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp) (the
pass) and [R/blp.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/blp.R).*

## 8. Willingness to Pay

### 8.1 Definition

When one covariate is a price $p$ with coefficient $\alpha = \beta_p$, the willingness to pay (WTP) for attribute $k$ is the marginal rate of substitution between the attribute and price — the price change that leaves utility unchanged after a unit change in the attribute:

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k = -\frac{\partial V / \partial x_k}{\partial V / \partial p} = -\frac{\beta_k}{\alpha}
$$

Since utility is linear, the same ratio applies to ASCs: the WTP for alternative $j$'s unobserved quality is $-\delta_j / \alpha$.

### 8.2 Delta-Method Standard Errors

WTP is a nonlinear function $g(\theta) = -\theta_k / \theta_p$ of the estimated coefficients. By the delta method, with $\hat{V}$ the estimated coefficient covariance matrix,

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(g(\hat\theta)) = \nabla g^T \, \hat{V}_{(k,p)} \, \nabla g,
\qquad
\nabla g = \begin{pmatrix} \partial g / \partial \theta_k \\ \partial g / \partial \theta_p \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} -1/\theta_p \\ \theta_k/\theta_p^2 \end{pmatrix}
$$

where $\hat{V}_{(k,p)}$ is the $2 \times 2$ block of $\hat{V}$ for $(\theta_k, \theta_p)$. The gradient is analytic (exact), so no numerical differentiation is involved. Confidence intervals use the normal approximation:

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k \pm z_{1-(1-\text{level})/2} \cdot \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}
$$

Because the estimates and covariance are stored in natural (unscaled) units, no scaling adjustment is needed even when the model was estimated with `scale_vars`.

**Caveat.** The ratio of two asymptotically normal estimators has heavy tails when the denominator is imprecisely estimated; the delta-method interval is a first-order approximation that deteriorates as $|\alpha| / \mathrm{SE}(\hat\alpha)$ falls. For a weakly identified price coefficient, simulation methods (Krinsky–Robb) or Fieller intervals are more reliable.

*Code reference: [R/wtp.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/wtp.R)*

## 9. Consumer Surplus and the Logsum

### 9.1 The Logsum (Expected Maximum Utility)

Under Type I Extreme Value errors, the expected maximum utility over individual $i$'s choice set is, up to an additive constant (Euler's constant $\gamma$):

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[\max_j U_{ij}\right] = \log\left(\sum_{j \in C_i} \exp(V_{ij})\right) + \gamma \equiv \mathrm{logsum}_i + \gamma
$$

When the model includes an outside option with normalized utility $V_{i0} = 0$, the sum includes its $\exp(0) = 1$ term. The implementation uses the same max-subtraction trick as the log-likelihood (Section 2.3).

### 9.2 Expected Consumer Surplus

With utility linear in price (no income effects), the marginal utility of income is $-\alpha$ (positive for a negative price coefficient), and expected consumer surplus in money units is (Train 2009, Ch. 3):

$$
\mathbb{E}[CS_i] = \frac{\mathrm{logsum}_i}{-\alpha}
$$

**Identification caveat.** Like utility itself, the logsum is only defined up to an additive normalization (in particular the ASC normalization), so CS *levels* are not interpretable on their own. The economically meaningful quantity is the *difference* between scenarios,

$$
\Delta \mathbb{E}[CS_i] = \frac{\mathrm{logsum}_i^{(1)} - \mathrm{logsum}_i^{(0)}}{-\alpha},
$$

computed by evaluating the logsum on counterfactual data (`newdata`) and on the baseline. The normalization constant cancels in the difference.
The routine does not impose $\alpha<0$; interpreting the denominator as positive marginal
utility of income requires the analyst to verify the fitted price sign.

### 9.3 Delta-Method SE for the Mean Consumer Surplus

For the weighted mean $m(\theta) = \sum_i w_i CS_i / \sum_i w_i$, the implementation reports a delta-method standard error. The building block is the derivative of the logsum, which by the envelope-style identity is a probability-weighted average of utility derivatives:

$$
\frac{\partial\, \mathrm{logsum}_i}{\partial \theta_r}
= \sum_{j \in C_i} P_{ij} \, \frac{\partial V_{ij}}{\partial \theta_r}
$$

with $\partial V_{ij}/\partial \beta_r = x_{ijr}$, $\partial V_{ij}/\partial \delta_a = \mathbf{1}_{j = a}$, and a zero contribution from the outside option row ($V_{i0} \equiv 0$). Then:

- For non-price parameters: $\dfrac{\partial CS_i}{\partial \theta_r} = \dfrac{1}{-\alpha} \dfrac{\partial\, \mathrm{logsum}_i}{\partial \theta_r}$.
- For the price coefficient, which enters both the logsum and the $1/(-\alpha)$ factor:

$$
\frac{\partial CS_i}{\partial \alpha}
= \frac{\mathrm{logsum}_i}{\alpha^2}
+ \frac{1}{-\alpha} \sum_{j} P_{ij}\, x_{ij,p}
$$

The SE is $\sqrt{G^T \hat{V} G}$, where $G$ is the weighted average of the per-individual gradient vectors and $\hat{V}$ the full coefficient covariance. All ingredients ($P_{ij}$, $V_{ij}$, $X$) come from a single prediction pass.

*Code reference: [R/surplus.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/surplus.R)*

## 10. Goodness of Fit

### 10.1 McFadden Pseudo R-Squared

$$
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\ell(\hat\theta)}{\ell_0},
\qquad
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \frac{\ell(\hat\theta) - K}{\ell_0}
$$

where $K$ is the number of estimated parameters and $\ell_0$ is a null-model log-likelihood. Two nulls are available:

**Equal shares** (default). Every alternative in individual $i$'s choice set is equally likely:

$$
\ell_0 = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \log\left(M_i + \mathbf{1}_{\text{outside}}\right)
$$

where $M_i$ is the number of inside alternatives. This closed form is exact for unbalanced choice sets and arbitrary weights.

**Market shares.** The maximized log-likelihood of a constants-only (ASC-only) model. When every alternative is available in every choice situation, the ASC-only model's fitted probabilities equal the observed market shares $s_j$, giving the closed form

$$
\ell_0 = c\sum_{j} N_j \log(s_j),
$$

with $N_j$ the unweighted choice counts and $c$ the common observation weight (usually
$c=1$ after normalization).  The outside option enters as its own category when present;
never-chosen alternatives contribute $0 \cdot \log 0 = 0$. This closed form requires
identical choice-set *composition* across individuals — equal set sizes are not sufficient
— and uniform weights; otherwise an ASC-only model must be refit explicitly.

### 10.2 Hit Rate

The hit rate is the weighted share of choice situations in which the observed choice has the highest predicted probability:

$$
\mathrm{HR} = \frac{\sum_i w_i \, \mathbf{1}\{\hat{j}_i = j_i\}}{\sum_i w_i},
\qquad
\hat{j}_i = \arg\max_{j \in C_i} P_{ij}
$$

With an outside option, the outside good competes for the maximum with probability $P_{i0} = 1 - \sum_j P_{ij}$, and a predicted outside choice is a hit when the outside good was in fact chosen ($j_i = 0$).
Ties among inside alternatives are resolved by the first local row (`which.max` in R).
The outside option replaces that inside winner only when its probability is strictly
larger, not when tied.

*Code reference: [R/gof.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/gof.R)*

---

## 11. Choice-Based Sampling and WESML Weighting

### 11.1 Endogenous Stratified (Choice-Based) Sampling

Under *random* (exogenous) sampling each choice situation is drawn independently of its
outcome. Under **choice-based** (endogenous stratified) sampling the strata are defined by
the **chosen alternative** $j_i$, and situations are drawn with stratum-specific
frequencies — for example, deliberately oversampling individuals who chose a rare
alternative. Let $Q(j)$ be the population share of alternative $j$ and $H(j)$ the sample
share of choosers of $j$.

For the multinomial logit there is a well-known special case: with a **full set of
alternative-specific constants**, choice-based sampling biases **only the constants**, and
the slope coefficients $\beta$ remain consistent (Manski & McFadden 1981). Outside that
case — most importantly when the ASCs are not saturated, or when the constants themselves
are of interest (welfare, counterfactual entry) — naive (unweighted) maximum likelihood is
**inconsistent for the population parameters**, and the weighting below is required.

### 11.2 The WESML Weighted Log-Likelihood

Manski and Lerman (1977) restore consistency by weighting each situation's contribution by
the ratio of population to sample share of its chosen alternative,

$$
w_i = \frac{Q(j_i)}{H(j_i)},
\qquad
\ell^{W}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i \log P_{i j_i}(\theta).
$$

The maximizer $\hat\theta$ is invariant to multiplying every $w_i$ by a common positive
constant, so the weights may be normalized to mean 1 without changing the estimates.

### 11.3 Robust (Sandwich) Variance: the $w^2$ Meat

WESML is a weighted M-estimator solving $\sum_i w_i\, s_i(\hat\theta) = 0$, where
$s_i = \partial \log P_{i j_i}/\partial\theta$ is the per-situation score ($\S$3) and
$H_i = \partial^2 \log P_{i j_i}/\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top$ its Hessian
($\S$4). Its robust (Huber–White) asymptotic variance is the **sandwich**

$$
V = A^{-1} B A^{-1}, \qquad
A = \sum_{i} w_i\,(-H_i), \qquad
B = \sum_{i} w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}.
$$

The weight enters the **bread** $A$ linearly, but the **meat** $B$ carries the weight
**squared**: the contribution of situation $i$ to the estimating equation is $w_i s_i$, so
the variance of that contribution involves $(w_i s_i)(w_i s_i)^{\top}
= w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}$.

This is exactly why the two naive variances are wrong under weighting:

- the inverse-Hessian $A^{-1}$ assumes the information-matrix equality $A = B$, which
  **fails** once the $w_i$ are non-degenerate;
- the ordinary BHHH/OPG $\big(\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}\big)^{-1}$ uses the weight to the
  *first* power, not the second.

A consistency check: rescaling all weights by a constant $c$ sends $A \to cA$ and
$B \to c^{2} B$, so $V \to (cA)^{-1}(c^{2}B)(cA)^{-1} = A^{-1}BA^{-1}$ — the sandwich is
**invariant** to the weight scale, whereas $A^{-1} \to c^{-1} A^{-1}$ is not.

### 11.4 Scope: Robust vs. Design-Based Variance

The estimator implemented here is the **robust weighted-M-estimator (Huber–White)
variance**, whose meat $B = \sum_i w_i^{2}\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ is uncentered. This is the
asymptotic variance under **variable-probability sampling** (each population unit sampled
independently with a stratum-dependent probability). Under a **fixed-quota** design the
design-based variance centers the scores within strata and may be smaller; that
stratum-centered estimator is **out of scope** here. See Manski & McFadden (1981) for the
design-based treatment and Cosslett (1981) for the asymptotically efficient
conditional-maximum-likelihood alternative.

### 11.5 Implementation and Cluster-Robust Extension

The meats come from compiled kernels that never form the $N\times p$ matrix of scores
($N$ situations by $p$ parameters): the BHHH kernel `mnl_bhhh_parallel()` adds
$w_i\,s_is_i^T$ over each situation's compact block (§4.3), with `weights = w` for the
BHHH information and `weights = w^2` for the robust meat, the **weight-free** score $s_i$
entering both. With the bread

$$
A=\texttt{mnl\_loglik\_hessian\_parallel}(\widehat\theta;w),
\qquad B=\texttt{mnl\_bhhh\_parallel}(\widehat\theta;w^2)=\sum_i w_i^2 s_is_i^T,
$$

the variance is $V=A^{-1}BA^{-1}$, computed equilibrated by two solves against the $LU$
factors of the equilibrated bread, without forming an inverse (§12.6). The fit-time
variance (`se_method`), `vcov(fit, type = )`, the recomputation of a variance dropped from
a fit and `wesml_vcov()` all compute it from the same kernels (`.assemble_score_vcov()`, or
`compute_hessian()` for a Hessian or BHHH variance recomputed lazily), so a fit's variance is
the one `vcov()` returns post hoc: bit for bit at one thread, and up to the last bits with
more, where the threads' shares of the situations change from call to call.

For cluster labels $g(i)$, `se_method = "cluster"` replaces the meat by

$$
B_{\mathrm{cluster}}
=\sum_g\left(\sum_{i:g(i)=g}w_is_i\right)
       \left(\sum_{i:g(i)=g}w_is_i\right)^T.
$$

`mnl_cluster_meat_parallel()` forms it without the score matrix either: the situations
sorted by cluster, each cluster's weighted compact scores summed over the parameters its
situations touch, its outer product added once the cluster ends. The sorted situations are
cut into about four chunks of similar row counts per thread, and a cluster that a chunk
boundary cuts is merged, in chunk order, after the parallel loop. The labels are checked
before any kernel runs.
No $G/(G-1)$ or other finite-cluster correction is applied.  Clustering changes the
estimated covariance, not the likelihood or point estimate. User-facing entry points:
`wesml_weights()`
computes the Manski--Lerman weights from the population shares $Q$, while
`sample_by_choice()` draws a choice-based sample and attaches those weights;
`run_mnlogit(..., se_method = "sandwich")`
estimates with the robust variance; `wesml_vcov()` returns it post hoc. Passing
`run_mnlogit(..., weights_col = )` collapses a row-level weight column to one weight per
choice situation (validated constant within `id`), and a provenance guard prevents a
WESML-labeled sample from being silently fit unweighted.

*Code reference: `mnl_bhhh_parallel()` / `mnl_cluster_meat_parallel()` in [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp); `.assemble_score_vcov()`, `.logit_meat()` and `.sandwich_combine()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R) (`.score_meat()` there forms the same meats from the score matrix of `mnl_scores_parallel()`, as the tests' reference); `equilibrated_sandwich()` in [src/vcov.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/vcov.cpp); `wesml_weights()` / `sample_by_choice()` in [R/sampling.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/sampling.R).*

## 12. Implementation Details

### 12.1 Parameter Vector Structure

The full parameter vector $\theta$ is organized as:

| Block | Indices | Length | Description |
|-------|---------|--------|-------------|
| $\beta$ | $[0, K)$ | $K$ | Coefficients for design matrix $X$ |
| $\delta$ | $[K, K + J_{asc})$ | $0$, $J-1$, or $J$ | Free alternative-specific constants |

where $J_{asc}=0$ when `use_asc = FALSE`, $J_{asc} = J - 1$ without outside
option (first ASC normalized to 0), or $J_{asc} = J$ with outside option.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

### 12.2 Data Organization

- **Design matrix $X$**: Stacked matrix of dimension $(\sum_i M_i) \times K$, where $M_i$ is the number of (inside) alternatives for individual $i$
- **Alternative indices**: 1-based indexing in R, converted to 0-based in C++
- **Choice indices**: 1-based *local row positions within each situation's block* for
  inside alternatives, 0 for the outside option when included
- **Prefix sums $S$**: Used for efficient indexing into the stacked data: $S_i = \sum_{j < i} M_j$

### 12.3 OpenMP Parallelization

The implementation parallelizes over choice situations using OpenMP:
- Each thread keeps its working arrays (utilities, probabilities, score differences, and a
  copy of a situation's covariate rows where Armadillo's product needs one) and local
  accumulators: the log-likelihood and gradient, or a packed upper triangle of the Hessian
  or BHHH matrix (§4.3; one thread adds into the result itself, and above the budget the
  threads share it). All are allocated before the parallel loop, once the kernel's memory
  estimate has been checked, so that no choice situation allocates
- The Hessian's and BHHH matrix's triangles are added after the loop in thread order (above
  the budget, the constants' entries atomically during it); the log-likelihood and gradient
  in an order that can vary between calls
- Dynamic scheduling balances the load, each dispatch handing a thread about 256 stacked
  rows, at least one situation (`schedule(dynamic, chunk)`; `CHOICER_CHUNK_ROWS` at
  compile time), so that situations of a few rows do not pay a dispatch each; fewer where
  the largest situation has more than eight times the mean rows, so that no dispatch holds
  more than about 2,048 rows whatever the situations' order
- The elasticity and diversion-ratio kernels (§5.3, §6.5) add each situation's terms into
  a $J \times J$ sum: one thread into the result itself, $T$ threads into copies of their
  own while those fit in 2 GiB (added up in thread order after the loop), and beyond that
  into the shared result atomically, each thread keeping the outside option's row and
  column, which every situation touches, to itself. Their memory (the result, the threads'
  copies and working arrays) is checked before anything is allocated, as the estimation
  kernels' is; with one thread the sums do not depend on the 2 GiB budget

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp)*

### 12.4 Negated Objectives

The likelihood/gradient kernel and analytical-Hessian kernel return, respectively:
- $-\ell(\theta)$ (negated log-likelihood)
- $-\nabla\ell(\theta)$ (negated gradient)
- $-\nabla^2\ell(\theta)$ (negated Hessian)

This is for compatibility with minimization routines (e.g., `nloptr`) that expect a loss function to minimize rather than a likelihood to maximize.

### 12.5 Finite-Value Guards

If a situation's chosen log probability is non-finite, the likelihood kernel substitutes
$-10^{10}$ for that contribution and emits one warning after leaving the OpenMP region.
If the assembled negated objective is still non-finite, it returns $10^{10}$ and a zero
gradient; isolated non-finite gradient entries are set to zero. These sentinels let a line
search backtrack from pathological trial parameters and are not part of the regular
finite-utility likelihood. The kernel's list also holds `overflow`, `TRUE` where it
replaced anything (a clamped log probability, the sentinel, a gradient entry set to
zero): the optimizers do not see it, and the polish (§12.7) rejects a trial point that
sets it.

*Code reference: [src/mnlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mnlogit.cpp); the flag, `logit_sanitize()` in [src/choicer_internal.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/choicer_internal.h)*

### 12.6 Inverting the Information

Every reported variance of $\hat\theta$ is the inverse of an estimate of the information
matrix, or a sandwich built on one: $V = \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ with $\mathcal{I}$ the negated
Hessian $-\nabla^2_\theta \ell(\hat\theta)$ of §4 (`se_method = "hessian"`) or the BHHH
matrix $\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ of §11.3 (`"bhhh"`), or $V = A^{-1} B A^{-1}$ with
the bread $A$ and meat $B$ of §11.3 (`"sandwich"`) or §11.5 (`"cluster"`). In the data's
units the diagonal of $\mathcal{I}$ can span many orders of magnitude: a covariate
measured in thousands next to one measured in thousandths, or the constant of an
alternative a handful of individuals chose next to that of one most chose. Inverted as it
is, such a matrix can be refused as computationally singular although only the units make
it so (`solve()` refuses a matrix whose estimated reciprocal condition number falls below
the machine epsilon, and the units alone can push it there), and a sandwich built on it
can lose digits. Every fit, whatever the coordinates its optimizer used (`scale_vars`;
§1.5 of the [mixed logit article](mixed_logit_math.html)), therefore inverts the
equilibrated matrix:

$$
V = D\,(D \mathcal{I} D)^{-1} D, \qquad
D = \mathrm{diag}(d), \quad d = 2^{\,\mathrm{round}(-\frac{1}{2}\log_2 |\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal{I})|)},
$$

with $\mathrm{diag}(\mathcal{I})$ the vector of the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{I}$ and
the functions applied elementwise: $d$ holds the powers of two nearest, on a log scale, to
the inverse square roots of the diagonal's magnitudes, with an entry of 1 where the
diagonal entry is zero or not finite and every entry clamped to $[2^{-500}, 2^{500}]$. For
the sandwich, $V = D\,V_D\,D$ with $V_D = (DAD)^{-1} (DBD) (DAD)^{-1}$ and $D$ from $A$.
Any $D$ leaves $V$ unchanged in exact arithmetic, and powers of two make the products with
$D$ exact too, barring overflow or underflow: only the $LU$ factorization and the solves
round (for the sandwich, also the symmetrization below), on a matrix whose diagonal is
within a factor of two of one in magnitude except where a diagonal entry is zero or not
finite, or an entry of $d$ is clamped. The magnitude of the diagonal is used so that an
information that is not positive definite (away from a maximum) is equilibrated too, and
its negative variances reported: their standard errors are `NA`, with a message.

$D \mathcal{I} D$ is formed in one working copy, which LAPACK factors in place ($LU$ with
partial pivoting) with `solve()`'s checks: a pivot that is exactly zero is an error, and
so, when every factor is finite, is a reciprocal condition number (estimated in the
1-norm) below the machine epsilon; either error leaves the fit without a variance, its
standard errors `NA`, with a message. The identity is then solved against the factors into
the result, as reference LAPACK's `dgesv` does for `solve()`, with two $p \times p$
matrices besides $\mathcal{I}$ ($p$ the number of parameters) where `solve()` holds three.
The sandwich is solved twice against the factors of $DAD$, first $(DAD)\,Y = DBD$ and then
the transposed system $(DAD)^{\top} V_D^{\top} = Y^{\top}$, without forming an inverse:
two $p \times p$ matrices besides $A$ and $B$ where an explicit inverse and two products
hold four, and $4\tfrac{2}{3} p^3$ operations against $6\tfrac{2}{3} p^3$. $V_D$ is
symmetrized, $(V_D + V_D^{\top})/2$, before $D$ is applied. At $p = 17{,}000$ each such
matrix takes 2.3 GB. The working copy is freed as the call returns, and the package's own
passes over whole matrices (the scaling, the scan of the factors for non-finite entries,
the transposition and the symmetrization) run in parallel over columns, without sums
across threads, so they do not depend on the number of threads. The fit and post-hoc
`vcov(fit, type = )` and `wesml_vcov()` take this same route.

Against an exact computation on the package's reference battery and tests (963 inversions
of 477 distinct matrices, of 2 to 13 parameters), a raw inversion refused 52 as singular;
equilibrated, 44 of them, with raw condition numbers from $4.5 \times 10^{18}$ to
$1.2 \times 10^{28}$, had condition numbers below 20 and came out with standard errors
within about $10^{-15}$ relative of exact, while the other eight stayed ill-conditioned or
singular. Equilibration removes the ill-conditioning that the parameters' units cause, not
the likelihood's own: a matrix that stays ill-conditioned after it (a likelihood nearly
flat along a combination of parameters, which no rescaling of the parameters one by one
removes) keeps only the digits its condition number allows, by any inversion, and one
singular to working precision is refused either way.

*Code reference: `invert_hessian()`, `.sandwich_combine()` and `.jacobi_scale()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R); `equilibrated_inverse()` and `equilibrated_sandwich()` in [src/vcov.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/vcov.cpp).*

### 12.7 Polishing the Optimizer's Solution

`run_mnlogit(polish = )` follows the optimizer with the Newton phase of the
[mixed logit](mixed_logit_math.html) (§5.7 there), which finishes the climb to the maximum
of the same log-likelihood and certifies it; the estimator does not change. With $g$ the
gradient of $-\ell$ and $C$ the curvature, the information $\mathcal{I} = -\nabla^2 \ell$
of §4 (`polish = "newton"`) or the BHHH matrix $\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^{\top}$ of §11.3
(`"bhhh"`, its weights unsquared), the polish converges when the Newton decrement

$$
\nu = \tfrac{1}{2}\, g^{\top} C^{-1} g,
$$

over the mean weight $\bar w$, falls below `tol_decrement` ($10^{-8}$). On a positive
definite $\mathcal{I}$ the remaining Newton step then moves every linear combination of the
estimates by at most $\sqrt{2\nu}$ of its Hessian standard error; with `"bhhh"` the bound
is in robust standard errors (for an unweighted fit; with weights, in the metric of
$\mathcal{I}^{-1} \mathcal{B} \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ with $\mathcal{B}$'s weights unsquared),
and a small BHHH decrement on its own shows only a stationary point. The steps, their damping and maximum length, and the line search are
those of the mixed logit's §5.7 (the multinomial logit has no bounds).

The multinomial logit's log-likelihood is concave: with $X_i$ the rows of situation $i$'s
design, the constants' indicators included, and $p_i$ its probabilities,
$\mathcal{I} = \sum_i w_i\, X_i^{\top} \big(\mathrm{diag}(p_i) - p_i p_i^{\top}\big) X_i$
is positive semidefinite everywhere. Wherever it is positive definite (the model
identified at the current point) and not singular to working precision, the Newton step
needs no damping, and the maximum the polish certifies is the global one.

A trial point fails where the likelihood kernel reports that its objective or gradient is
not the log-likelihood's (§12.5): a chosen log probability clamped to $-10^{10}$, a total
that is not finite, or a gradient entry set to zero. The constant of an alternative never
chosen has a negative score at every $\theta$, and that of one chosen wherever it is
offered a positive one, so neither has a finite estimate (`run_mnlogit()` warns of them);
the polish holds the constants of such inside alternatives at the optimizer's values, and
the certificate concerns the other parameters given them. Where the reference itself (the
base alternative, or the outside option) is the one without, the other constants diverge
together, and the polish does not report convergence unless the reference is never chosen
and the held constants anchor all the others, which stops their rise. An alternative is
anchored if its constant is held, or if it is offered in a choice situation whose chosen
alternative is anchored. With every constant that can rise anchored, any direction of the
constants that raises a set of them meets the situation that anchored the member of the
set anchored first; there the chosen alternative, outside the set, has a probability that
falls to zero, and with it the log-likelihood. A held alternative chosen only where it is
offered alone anchors nothing.

The polish's maximum step and its stall rule are measured in the optimizer's coordinates
$m$ (§1.5 of the mixed logit article). Under `scale_vars = "none"` those would be the
parameters' own units, in which a column measured in thousandths needs coefficient steps
of hundreds, so the scales come instead from the BHHH diagonal at the optimizer's solution,
as `"bhhh"` takes them at the start values: one pass of the gradient kernel. The variance
is computed at the polished estimates, by `se_method`, and the polish's last curvature,
evaluated at the point it returns, is not evaluated again where it is the variance's own
matrix: after `"newton"` the Hessian of `"hessian"` and the bread of `"sandwich"` and
`"cluster"`, after `"bhhh"` the BHHH matrix of `"bhhh"`.

On census- and claims-style designs (2,504 and 2,602 alternatives with 24,560 and 245,031
choice situations; 499 and 500 alternatives with 17,339 and 153,721 situations; ten
covariates; constants without a finite estimate removed; single runs at eleven threads,
times modeled from the kernels' calls) the default fit (`scale_vars = "bhhh"`) stopped at
the maximum in 29 to 42 evaluations, and the Newton polish certified it at once: with its
Hessian serving the variance, it added one gradient pass and one Cholesky factorization, 3
to 13% of the modeled time of the fit and its variance. With `scale_vars = "none"` the
optimizer stopped up to 9.2 log-likelihood units short, at its limit of 1,000 evaluations
on three of the designs, and the polish closed the gap in 1 to 6 steps. With half of the
covariates rescaled by $10^3$ and the other half by $10^{-3}$, 20 steps at unit scales left
a decrement of 1,130 to 2,060, where 8 or 9 at the BHHH scales certified the maximum.

*Code reference: `run_polish()`, `.polish_held()`, `.polish_anchors()`, `.polish_fit()`
and `.polish_scales()` in [R/classes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/classes.R);
`newton_step()` in [src/newton.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/newton.cpp);
the curvature and its reuse in `run_mnlogit()`,
[R/mnlogit_utils.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/mnlogit_utils.R);
the kernel's report, `logit_sanitize()` in
[src/choicer_internal.h](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/choicer_internal.h).*
